484.title: The lowest of all
484.hook: whoever knows himself lowest of all is counted highest (Sukhmani 12)
484.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water for Guru Angad as a model of seva, and in gurdwaras today volunteers wash dishes, sweep and mind shoes, often without anyone knowing their names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the proud fall, and your line: pride falls. Did you keep one good deed to yourself? Today the same ashtpadi flips the ladder upside down. Day four hundred eighty-four.

Sikh tradition tells of an old man who carried water. Every morning before dawn, for years, he walked to the river, filled a pitcher, and brought it back for his teacher, Guru Angad, to bathe. One dark, stormy morning he tripped near a weaver's house and fell into the pit where the loom stood. The weaver's wife heard the noise and said, more or less: that's only Amru, the man with no home, who wanders around after his guru. A nobody. That nobody was the man who became the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. Today Sukhmani gives the rule his life was following.
screen: `AN OLD MAN CARRIES WATER.` → `HE FALLS. ONLY AMRU, A NOBODY.` → `THE NOBODY BECOMES THE THIRD GURU.`

segments.voice: Near the end of the twelfth ashtpadi's first stanza, after all the prides, Guru Arjan turns the ladder over. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa. Whoever knows himself to be low is counted the highest of all. Two words carry the line. Neechaa: low, beneath. Oochaa: high, above. They're ordinary Punjabi, words for a shelf or a hill. And the verb in the middle matters: ganeeai, is counted, is reckoned. The line doesn't say the humble person feels high, or gets promoted at work. It says that in the real reckoning, God's count, the order is reversed. The next line deepens it: the one whose mind becomes the dust of all recognizes the Name in every heart. That's the reason the low place works. When you're not looking down on anyone, you can finally see what's in them. Back to the story. Tradition says when Guru Angad heard what the weaver's wife had called Amar Das, the homeless one, he answered by calling him the home of the homeless, the honor of those without honor. The insult turned into a title. Amar Das was in his seventies when he became Guru, and many Sikhs remember that among the first things he insisted on was the langar: whoever wanted to see him, a king included, first ate sitting on the floor with everyone else. The lowest seat, made into the door. So this isn't a trick for getting ahead, being humble now to be on top later. The stanza is describing how things are already counted. We just can't see the scoreboard.
screen: `NEECHAA: LOW. OOCHAA: HIGH.` · `COUNTED, NOT FELT.` · `THE DUST OF ALL SEES EVERY HEART.` · `HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · then, large: `LOWEST IS HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve someone quietly, in your mind first. Think of one person whose day you could make easier, a roommate, a coworker, someone at home. Picture one small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: the dishes, a refilled water jug, a door held. Picture yourself doing it and walking away without a word. Let that feel like enough. Then, if it's possible today, do it. The bell holds the time.
The lowest of all. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa: whoever knows himself low is counted highest, the way an old water carrier became the third Guru.
Your line: lowest is highest. Do one helpful thing today that nobody will thank you for, and don't mention it. Day four hundred eighty-four.

485.title: Living ashtpadi 12
485.hook: humility is the doorway to every virtue in Sukhmani
485.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the twelfth ashtpadi's warnings about the I that claims to be the doer, and in many gurdwaras Asa di Var, with its line on sweetness and humility, is sung each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lowest of all, and your line: lowest is highest. Did you do one thankless helpful thing? Today we close the twelfth ashtpadi by living it. Day four hundred eighty-five.
screen: `THE LOWEST OF ALL — LOWEST IS HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Two words, said badly or said well, can change a whole evening: I'm sorry. Most of us know exactly how hard they are. You rehearse them in the car. You add a but. You explain why it wasn't really your fault before you get to the part where it was. The apology gets stuck somewhere between the throat and the pride. And then, when someone finally says it plainly, no but, no speech, something in the room loosens. Sukhmani has spent a whole ashtpadi on why that loosening happens. Today: humility, put first.
screen: `I'M SORRY. TWO WORDS.` → `REHEARSED, STUCK, WITH A BUT.` → `SAID PLAINLY, THE ROOM LOOSENS.`

segments.voice: Look at where the twelfth ashtpadi sits. Sukhmani is twenty-four ashtpadis long, and this one lands near the middle of the hymn. Before it, Guru Arjan has talked about remembering the Name, about the company of the holy, about the One who does everything. Here he stops and names the thing all of that depends on. In the second stanza of this ashtpadi, he puts it this way, in paraphrase: as long as a person thinks, something gets done by me, there's no peace for them. As long as a person thinks, I am the doer, they keep going round and round. The I is the blockage. While it's in the doorway, nothing else can come through. That's why many Sikhs call humility the doorway to the other virtues. Guru Nanak had already said something like it in Asa di Var, a hymn sung in many gurdwaras every morning: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtue and goodness. Mithat neevee, in Punjabi. Sweetness, and lowness. Notice the pair. Humility in Sikh teaching is never sour. It isn't a grim, hunched-over feeling of being nothing. It's sweet: easy to be around, quick to laugh, quick to say sorry. And that's the living part. An apology is humility in the smallest possible size. It says: I was the doer of this, and it wasn't right. Strangely, owning the mistake is the opposite of pride, because pride's whole job is to defend the self. So the twelfth ashtpadi lands somewhere very ordinary: a kitchen, a car, a group chat, wherever two people have just rubbed each other the wrong way. Humility first, and then everything else has room.
screen: `THE MIDDLE OF SUKHMANI.` · `WHILE I AM THE DOER, NO PEACE.` · `MITHAT NEEVEE: SWEET AND LOW.` · `SORRY: HUMILITY, SMALL SIZE.` · then, large: `HUMILITY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the apology you owe. Sit still and let the past week drift by: a sharp word, a late reply, a promise that slipped. Don't go hunting for big guilt. Look for one small thing where you were the doer and it wasn't right. When you find it, say the words silently, plainly, with no but on the end: I'm sorry. Feel how short the sentence is. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 12. Humility as the doorway: while I am the doer blocks it, nothing else comes through. Mithat neevee, sweetness and lowness, together.
Your line: humility first. Today, say sorry once, out loud, to the person you owe it to, and stop after the word sorry. Day four hundred eighty-five.

486.title: Ashtpadi 13, salok: the holy
486.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach the thirteenth ashtpadi's salok on the sant, and Sikh life places great weight on sangat, the company of the good, in shared prayer, singing and the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 12, and your line: humility first. Did you manage a plain sorry, with nothing after it? Today a new ashtpadi, the thirteenth, and a new stretch of Sukhmani. Day four hundred eighty-six.

Who's the best person you actually know? Not the most famous, not the most impressive. The best. Maybe a neighbor who shovels the whole block's sidewalks and never mentions it. An aunt who remembers every birthday. A nurse who stayed after her shift. Most of us can name one or two straight away. And most of us have never told them. We praise celebrities in public and the truly good people in our lives almost never. The salok of the thirteenth ashtpadi starts right there: with the good ones, and what it means to stand near them.
screen: `THE BEST PERSON YOU KNOW.` → `NOT FAMOUS. GOOD.` → `AND YOU'VE NEVER TOLD THEM.`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines, and they pull in opposite directions. The first, in paraphrase: whoever takes shelter with the saints is carried across. The second: whoever slanders the saints, Nanak, is born again and again. Today we stay with the first line; tomorrow the ashtpadi turns to the second, and spends a long time there. First, the word. Sant. It's usually translated saint, but be careful. In the Guru Granth Sahib a sant isn't someone a council has declared holy, with a feast day or a statue. A sant is a person whose life is soaked in remembering God: honest, humble, kind, steady. Sukhmani has already described such people in earlier ashtpadis, the holy company and the God-conscious one. They might run a shop. They might be your grandmother. Next, the verb: saran. Shelter, refuge, the way you'd step under an awning when it rains. The salok isn't asking you to worship good people. It's saying that nearness to them changes you. Sikhs call it sangat, the company, and much of Sikh life is built around it: praying together, singing together, eating together in the langar. Goodness, in this picture, is catching. You stand near it long enough and some of it rubs off, the way a cloth takes on the scent of the flowers it's wrapped around. Then the second line hangs over the first like a cloud: if nearness lifts you, contempt for the good drags you down. That's tomorrow. Today's job is simpler. Notice the good people. Honor them.
screen: `TWO LINES, OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS.` · `SANT: A LIFE SOAKED IN THE NAME.` · `SARAN: SHELTER UNDER AN AWNING.` · `GOODNESS IS CATCHING.` · then, large: `HONOR THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a good person. Bring one to mind, someone whose goodness is quiet. See their face. Remember one specific thing they did, a small one is best. Hold it there and let yourself be grateful that people like this exist. Then, if you like, picture telling them so, in one plain sentence. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 13. Its salok honors the sant, the person soaked in remembering God, and says shelter near such people carries you across.
Your line: honor the good. Today, tell one good person, out loud or in a message, one specific thing you admire about them. Day four hundred eighty-six.

487.title: The harm of slander
487.hook: slandering the holy spoils the slanderer's own life (Sukhmani 13)
487.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the thirteenth ashtpadi's repeated lines beginning sant kai dookhan, and nindaa, slander, is warned against throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 13, and your line: honor the good. Did you tell one good person what you admire in them? Today the salok's second line takes over the whole ashtpadi. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

A group chat, late at night. Someone posts a screenshot of a coworker's message and adds an eye-roll. Within a minute there are six replies. Everyone has a story. Nobody is lying exactly, but by the end the coworker is a joke, and the chat has never been livelier. It feels good, in a sour sort of way. You go to sleep a little buzzed and a little worse. Guru Arjan spends an entire ashtpadi on that buzz, and he keeps asking one question that the group chat never does: what is this doing to us?
screen: `A SCREENSHOT AND AN EYE-ROLL.` → `SIX REPLIES IN A MINUTE.` → `WHAT IS THIS DOING TO US?`

segments.voice: The thirteenth ashtpadi is built like a drumbeat. Line after line begins with the same three words: sant kai dookhan. Through harming the holy, through speaking ill of them. And then each line names a cost. Through slandering the holy, the text says, life is cut short. Through slandering the holy, all peace goes. The mind becomes dirty. Honor is lost. No one comes to help. The list keeps going, stanza after stanza, the same opening words returning like a knock on a door. Now look at who pays in every single line. Not the sant. The good person being slandered is never the one who suffers in these stanzas. The losses all fall on the slanderer: their peace, their mind, their standing, their life. That's the surprise in this ashtpadi, and it turns the group chat upside down. We gossip because it seems to cost the other person something and give us something: a laugh, a bond, a bit of height. Sukhmani says the accounts run the other way. The one being talked about loses very little. The one talking is the one being emptied. Two words are worth holding. Dookhan, from dookh, pain or fault: speaking ill, finding fault, doing harm with words. And nindaa, the most common word in Gurbani for slander, which the salok uses. And why the holy, especially? Because, as yesterday's salok said, nearness to the good lifts us. Slander is the opposite of nearness. It pushes the good away from us on purpose, and with them, the very company that might have carried us across.
screen: `SANT KAI DOOKHAN: A DRUMBEAT.` · `LINE AFTER LINE, A COST.` · `THE SLANDERER ALWAYS PAYS.` · `PUSHING THE GOOD AWAY.` · then, large: `SLANDER HARMS THE SLANDERER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say nothing unkind, even inside. For these two minutes, sit and let the mind do what it does. It will probably bring up someone who annoys you and start a little commentary. When it does, don't argue with it. Just stop the sentence halfway, like lifting a needle off a record. Breathe out. Wait for the next one. You're not forcing kindness yet; you're only learning where the needle is. The bell holds the time.
The harm of slander. Sant kai dookhan: in the thirteenth ashtpadi, line after line, the one who speaks ill of the good is the one who pays.
Your line: slander harms the slanderer. Today, say nothing unkind about anyone who isn't in the room. If a conversation turns that way, let your reply be silence. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

488.title: What slander does inside
488.hook: slander darkens the one who speaks it (Sukhmani 13)
488.howItsDone: Sikhs end the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of daily worship and many gatherings, with a line asking for sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all; Sukhmani's thirteenth ashtpadi names slander's inner stain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harm of slander, and your line: slander harms the slanderer. Did you let one unkind conversation pass in silence? Today we look inside the one who speaks, and at what to put there instead. Day four hundred eighty-eight.
screen: `THE HARM OF SLANDER — SLANDER HARMS THE SLANDERER.`

segments.voice: Ever notice how a complaint grows when you tell it? The first time, it's a small thing your brother said. By the third retelling, it has a beginning, a middle and a villain. You've rehearsed it so often you can feel it in your jaw. The brother has long since forgotten. You haven't, because you've been carrying it around and polishing it. Slander works like that on the inside. It doesn't stay out there, in the story. It moves in. Today: what slander does inside the one who speaks it, and the one small word Sikhs put in its place.
screen: `A COMPLAINT GROWS EACH TELLING.` → `YOU FEEL IT IN YOUR JAW.` → `SLANDER MOVES IN.`

segments.voice: Among the costs in the thirteenth ashtpadi, one goes deeper than the rest. Through slandering the holy, the text says, the mind becomes maleen: dirty, stained, like cloth dipped in mud. It's an inside cost. Not a punishment arriving later, but a change happening right now, in the person speaking. Every time you rehearse someone's faults, you're the one marinating in them. The Guru Granth Sahib has a famous picture of this from the other side. The poet-saint Kabir, whose hymns sit in the scripture beside the Gurus', says something startling: let people slander me; the slanderer is actually my helper. Why? Because, in Kabir's image, the slanderer washes my dirty clothes for me. My faults move off me and onto their tongue. It's funny and a little unsettling, and it says the same thing as Sukhmani: the dirt ends up with the one who talks. So what goes in its place? Sikhs have an answer they say every day. The Ardas, the standing prayer said at the end of so much of Sikh worship, closes with a line that ends sarbat da bhalaa. The good of all. The well-being of everyone, with no list of exceptions. Not my family, my side, the people I like: sarbat, all. People who say Ardas daily are, every day, wishing well to the very people they might be tempted to slander. That's the swap. Not just stopping the unkind word, which leaves an empty space. Filling the space with a blessing. A stained cloth doesn't get clean by being left alone. It gets clean by being washed.
screen: `THE MIND MADE MALEEN: STAINED.` · `KABIR: THE SLANDERER WASHES ME.` · `ARDAS: SARBAT DA BHALAA.` · `FILL THE SPACE WITH A BLESSING.` · then, large: `BLESS INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: swap one criticism for a blessing. Bring to mind one person you've been criticizing lately, out loud or just in your head. Notice the complaint, the polished story. Now set it down. In its place, wish them one plain good thing: that they sleep well tonight, that their work goes right, that they're less worried than they seem. If you pray, you can hold them inside sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all. The bell holds the time.
What slander does inside. It stains the speaker's own mind, maleen; and the Ardas puts sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all, in its place.
Your line: bless instead. Today, every time you catch a criticism forming about someone, follow it with one silent good wish for them. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

489.title: Living ashtpadi 13
489.howItsDone: Gurbani returns often to the rasnaa, the tongue, and to the sweetness of speaking the Name; many Sikhs take Sukhmani's warnings on slander, and Guru Nanak's line on harsh words, as a daily guard on gossip.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what slander does inside, and your line: bless instead. Did a criticism turn into a good wish even once? Today we take the thirteenth ashtpadi out of the hymn and into an ordinary day. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

Try counting, just for one lunch break, how much of the talk around you is about people who aren't there. Who's dating whom. Who got the promotion and didn't deserve it. What the neighbor is doing with that yard. Most of it isn't cruel. It's just the easy, warm currency of being together. And that's what makes it hard: gossip isn't usually a decision. It's a habit of the tongue, running ahead of us. Sukhmani's thirteenth ashtpadi warned about slander of the holy. Living it means watching the smaller cousin, the one that shows up at lunch.
screen: `COUNT THE TALK AT LUNCH.` → `ABOUT PEOPLE WHO AREN'T THERE.` → `A HABIT OF THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Gurbani has a word for the tongue that shows up again and again: rasnaa. It comes from ras, taste, juice, flavor. The tongue is the tasting organ, and the Gurus play with that. What the tongue keeps tasting, it gets a taste for. Many hymns speak of a tongue that savors the Name, that has found the sweetest flavor and wants nothing else. The opposite is a tongue that has acquired a taste for other people's faults, and keeps going back for more. Guru Nanak puts it bluntly in Asa di Var, the hymn we met a few days ago: speaking harsh, tasteless words, the body and mind themselves become tasteless. The word is phikaa. Bland, flat, insipid, like food with no salt. It's a striking picture. Unkind talk doesn't just wound someone else; it drains the flavor out of the person talking. Put that beside the thirteenth ashtpadi and the shape is clear. Slander of the holy stains the mind. Everyday gossip, its small cousin, flattens it. Both start on the tongue. So why guard the tongue rather than the thoughts? Because the tongue is where a passing thought becomes a habit. A thought about someone's faults can drift by. Said out loud, it gets an audience, a laugh, a reply, and comes back stronger tomorrow. Guarding the tongue is like putting a gate at the end of a path: the thoughts may still wander up to it, but they don't get out into the world. And for a whole day, that gate can change more than you expect.
screen: `RASNAA: THE TASTING TONGUE.` · `A TASTE FOR THE NAME, OR FOR FAULTS.` · `PHIKAA: HARSH WORDS MAKE YOU BLAND.` · `A GATE AT THE END OF THE PATH.` · then, large: `GUARD THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest the tongue. Close your mouth gently and let the tongue lie soft against the floor of your mouth, not pressing anywhere. Notice how much it wants to move, even in silence: the tiny shapes of words forming. Each time you feel it start to shape a word, let it go soft again. Two minutes of a quiet tongue. If you pray, you can let it hold one word only, Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 13. Rasnaa, the tongue that tastes: it can learn a taste for the Name or for faults, and harsh words leave the speaker phikaa, flavorless.
Your line: guard the tongue. Try a whole day without gossip. When talk turns to someone who isn't there, change the subject, or say something good about them. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

490.title: Ashtpadi 14, salok: give up cleverness
490.hook: taj siaanap: give up cleverness and remember the Lord (Sukhmani 14)
490.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the fourteenth ashtpadi with the salok beginning taj siaanap, give up cleverness, and many read it as a turn from scheming toward a single hope in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 13, and your line: guard the tongue. How did a day without gossip go? It's the end of a week that went low and stayed there: lowest is highest, humility first, honor the good, slander harms the slanderer, bless instead, guard the tongue. Today, the fourteenth ashtpadi. Day four hundred ninety.

You're in the shower, rehearsing. If I say this to my boss, then she'll say that, and then I'll mention the other thing, and that way it looks like it was her idea. Version two. Version three. The water runs, the plan gets cleverer and cleverer, and somewhere around version five you notice that you're not actually solving anything. You're just circling. The fourteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with a two-word instruction for exactly that state: taj siaanap. Today: give up the cleverness.
screen: `IN THE SHOWER, REHEARSING.` → `VERSION TWO. VERSION FIVE.` → `TAJ SIAANAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok, in paraphrase. Give up your cleverness, good people, and remember the Lord, the King. Keep in your mind hope in the One alone. Then, Nanak, pain, doubt and fear depart. Taj: give up, let go, abandon. Siaanap: cleverness. It comes from siaanaa, a Punjabi word that can mean wise, but also shrewd, crafty, the one who always has an angle. And that second sense is the one the salok means. Be careful here, because this is easy to misread. Sukhmani isn't against thinking. Guru Nanak praised the person who reflects on learning, and Sikh history is full of scholars, poets and builders. Siaanap is something narrower: the scheming mind, the one that's always calculating how to come out on top, how to arrange people, how to secure every outcome in advance. Why let that go? Look at what the salok promises in its place. Three things depart: dookh, pain; bharam, doubt; and bhau, fear. That's a precise list, and it's the list of what the scheming mind produces. The shower plan isn't really about the boss. It's fear, wearing a clever coat. The more angles you calculate, the more angles there are to be afraid of. The salok's alternative is simple to say and hard to do: one hope, kept in the mind, ek aas. Not a dozen backup plans, each with its own worry attached. One place to rest. Tomorrow and the next day the ashtpadi will turn to where that hope should and shouldn't rest. Today, only the first move: put the clever plan down.
screen: `TAJ: LET GO. SIAANAP: CLEVERNESS.` · `NOT THINKING, BUT SCHEMING.` · `PAIN, DOUBT AND FEAR DEPART.` · `EK AAS: ONE HOPE.` · then, large: `DROP THE CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one scheme. Bring to mind a plan you've been circling, a conversation you keep rehearsing, an outcome you're trying to arrange. Hold it for a moment and see it clearly, all its versions. Then, on an out-breath, set it down. You can still act tomorrow; you're only putting down the circling. Rest in one simple hope instead of ten clever angles. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 14. Its salok: taj siaanap, give up your cleverness, keep one hope, and pain, doubt and fear depart.
Your line: drop the cleverness. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing an angle, stop and ask: what's the plain, straight version of this? Day four hundred ninety.
